title: 48 Hours Shooting in Lisbon (behind the scenes of my biggest client job)
creator: Tess Okafor
description:
Two very early mornings, one very patient art director, and a lot of tiles.

A few people asked how a commercial shoot actually runs, so here's a full day of one, minus the final photos (those belong to the client).

Shot on Sony A7 IV + 35mm f/1.4, vlog on a Pocket 3.
Music: my friend Rui's band, Maré Baixa.

Instagram: @tess.okafor

0:00 Six forty a.m.
0:40 Why I'm here
1:30 Chasing the light
2:40 The permit guy
3:30 Golden hour + wrap

sentences.t: Okay, good morning from Lisbon, it is six forty and I have had exactly one coffee.
We are up this early because the light on these tiles is only good for about an hour.
So, a little bit of context, because a bunch of you asked on Instagram why I'm back here again.
This trip is actually a work trip, I'm here shooting a campaign for Monos.
They're the luggage company, and their team hired me to shoot their spring lookbook.
It's a paid job, it's genuinely the biggest client I've ever had, and I am a little bit terrified.
The brief is basically suitcases in front of pretty doors, which sounds easy until you actually try it.
Their art director sent me a forty page mood board last week and I've read it maybe nine times.
I'm not going to show you any of the actual photos, obviously, they own those, that's how it works.
But I can show you how the day runs, which is the part I always wanted to see when I was starting out.
So this is Alfama, and this street right here is the whole reason we're up at dawn.
See how the sun comes straight down the hill and hits that blue wall?
That's the shot, that's the money shot, and we have maybe forty minutes before a tour group shows up.
My assistant today is Joana, say hi Joana.
She's holding the reflector, which is the most thankless job on any set, I promise you.
Okay, first setup, I'm on the thirty five, f two point eight, because I want a little bit of the street in focus.
If I go wide open the doors turn into soup and the client wants you to see the doors.
Joana, can you bring that up, a little more, more, perfect, don't move, don't breathe.
Oh no, there's a cat.
There's a cat sitting exactly on the mark.
Okay, it's nine fifteen now and the light is gone, like completely gone.
We got three setups out of the morning, which is one more than I planned, so I'm happy.
Now, the fun part, a man from the city council just walked up and asked for our permit.
And thank god the production team sorted that weeks ago, because I would not have known what to say in Portuguese.
This is a thing nobody tells you about client work, by the way.
Half of it is photography and the other half is paperwork, insurance, permits, release forms, all of it.
If you're a newer photographer and someone offers you a commercial job, ask who's handling permits before you say yes.
Okay, lunch, we're getting bifanas, which is basically a pork sandwich and it's the best thing in this city.
During lunch I'm going through the morning's shots on the laptop and flagging the ones I like.
I send a small batch to the art director so she can tell me if we're on track before the afternoon.
She came back with one note, which was more sky, which, fair.
So for golden hour we're going up to a viewpoint, the miradouro, where you get the whole river behind you.
This is the shot I'm most nervous about, because the wind up here is unreal.
Like, the model's hair is doing a thing and I can't decide if it's beautiful or chaos.
I'm going to bracket this, three exposures, so I can blend the sky later if I need to.
Okay, okay, okay, that one, that's it, I think that's the frame.
I can't show it to you, but trust me, I made a little noise when it came up on the screen.
And that's a wrap on day one.
My feet hurt, my face is sunburnt on one side only, and I'm so happy.
Tomorrow is a smaller day, just two locations, and then I get one free afternoon before my flight.
I'll probably vlog that part too, if I can stay awake.
Thanks for hanging out on a work day with me, see you in the next one.
